context: Regulation 6A: Notwithstanding anything contained in these regulations, no person who is a wilful defaulter shall make a public announcement of an open offer for acquiring shares or enter into any transaction that would attract the obligation to make a public announcement of an open offer for acquiring shares under these regulations. question: What does Regulation 6A of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 prohibit, and what exception does it carve out for wilful defaulters?
reference_answer: Regulation 6A prohibits wilful defaulters from making a public announcement of an open offer or entering into any transaction triggering an open offer obligation. reference_answer: Under Regulation 10(f), no scheme of an AIF shall have more than one thousand investors. Accredited investors are explicitly excluded from the computation of this investor count — meaning the 1,000-investor cap applies only to non-accredited investors.

context: Regulation 22(1): An individual investment adviser shall not provide distribution services. (2) The family of an individual investment adviser shall not provide distribution services to the client advised by the individual investment adviser and no individual investment adviser shall provide advice to a client who is receiving distribution services from other family members.
question: Can an individual investment adviser registered under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013 simultaneously provide distribution services to clients? Can the adviser's spouse provide distribution services to those same clients?
reference_answer: No on both counts. Under Regulation 22(1), an individual investment adviser is prohibited from providing distribution services. Under Regulation 22(2), the family of an individual investment adviser (which includes the spouse) cannot provide distribution services to the same clients advised by the individual investment adviser. Moreover, the individual investment adviser cannot provide advice to clients who are receiving distribution services from family members.

question: Institution X holds 12% of the shares of CRA-1. It proposes to acquire a 9% stake in CRA-2. Would this acquisition violate Regulation 24A(2) of the SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
reference_answer: No, the proposed acquisition would not violate Regulation 24A(2). The restriction applies to a shareholder holding 10% or more in one CRA acquiring 10% or more in another CRA. Institution X already holds 12% (≥10%) in CRA-1. However, the proposed acquisition in CRA-2 is only 9%, which is below the 10% threshold. Since the combined holding in CRA-2 (9%) is less than 10%, the restriction under Regulation 24A(2) is not triggered. The acquisition is permissible.

context: Regulation 24(4): All rating decisions, including the decisions regarding changes in rating, shall be taken by the rating committee. (8) A credit rating agency shall not rate securities issued by it.
question: Who has the authority to take rating decisions (including rating changes) under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Can a CRA rate its own securities?
reference_answer: Under Regulation 24(4), all rating decisions — including decisions on changes in rating — must be taken by the rating committee. Individual analysts or management cannot unilaterally assign or change ratings. Under Regulation 24(8), a CRA is explicitly prohibited from rating securities issued by itself.

context: Regulation 13(h): the number of clients of a part-time investment adviser shall not exceed seventy-five in total at any point of time.
question: A part-time investment adviser currently serves 68 clients. They plan to onboard 8 new clients in the coming week. After onboarding all 8 clients, how many total clients will the adviser have, and by how many would this exceed the regulatory limit? How many of the planned new clients can be legitimately onboarded?
reference_answer: Proposed total: 68 + 8 = 76 clients. The regulatory limit under Regulation 13(h) is 75 clients. Excess: 76 − 75 = 1 client. The adviser would exceed the limit by 1. Therefore, only 7 of the 8 planned new clients can be legitimately onboarded (68 + 7 = 75 = limit). The 8th client cannot be onboarded.

context: Regulation 15(1) (pre-2018): Every credit rating agency shall, during the lifetime of securities rated by it continuously monitor the rating of such securities. Regulation 15(1) (as substituted by SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018, w.e.f. 30-05-2018): Every credit rating agency shall, during the lifetime of securities rated by it continuously monitor the rating of such securities, unless the rating is withdrawn, subject to the provisions of regulation 16(3).
question: What change did the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 make to the continuous monitoring obligation under Regulation 15(1)?
reference_answer: The SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 (w.e.f. 30-05-2018) added a qualifying carveout to the continuous monitoring obligation in Regulation 15(1). The original version required CRAs to continuously monitor ratings 'during the lifetime of securities rated by it' with no exception. The 2018 amendment added the phrase 'unless the rating is withdrawn, subject to the provisions of regulation 16(3)' — clarifying that the monitoring obligation ceases if and when a rating is legitimately withdrawn in accordance with the conditions specified in Regulation 16(3) (i.e., winding up, merger, or as specified by the Board).

question: Under SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008, within how many days must SEBI dispose of a complete prior approval request for change in status or constitution? What is deemed to happen if SEBI fails to communicate its decision within this period?
reference_answer: Sixty days. If SEBI fails to communicate within sixty days, prior approval shall be deemed to have been granted.

question: An individual investment adviser currently has 287 clients. Over the next month, 18 new clients are onboarded. How many total clients does the adviser now have, and by how many clients does this exceed the regulatory threshold that triggers mandatory transition to non-individual status?
reference_answer: Total clients after onboarding: 287 + 18 = 305. The regulatory threshold under Regulation 13(e) is 300 clients. Excess above threshold: 305 − 300 = 5 clients. context: Where the certificate was granted for a specified period, an application for grant of certificate under sub-regulation (1) shall be made by the intermediary at least three months prior to the expiry of such period or three months prior to expiry of two years from the commencement of these regulations in relation to such intermediary, whichever is earlier and if the intermediary fails to do so, it shall cease to act as an intermediary on and from the expiry of the aforementioned period.
question: An intermediary's time-limited certificate expires in 18 months from the commencement of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008. Under this provision, when is the earliest date by which it must apply for renewal?
reference_answer: The intermediary must apply at least three months before the earlier of: (a) expiry of the certificate (15 months from commencement), or (b) three months before two years from commencement (21 months). reference_answer: No. Under Regulation 2(1)(ab)(ii), a body corporate must have a net worth of at least Rs 50 crore to qualify as an accredited investor. With a net worth of Rs 45 crore, the body corporate falls short by Rs 5 crore (Rs 50 crore − Rs 45 crore = Rs 5 crore). It does not qualify as an accredited investor.

question: In Illustration 3 of the RBI SFB Dividend Directions 2026, the bank paid interim dividend during FY 20X1-X2 before declaring the final dividend. What does this sequencing imply about when the Maximum Eligible Dividend constraint applies — at the time of the interim dividend, or cumulatively across both payments?
reference_answer: The constraint applies cumulatively across both payments. The Maximum Eligible Dividend (₹1,125 crore) is the total permitted across the full financial year. Since ₹500 crore has already been paid as interim dividend, the final dividend is capped at the remaining ₹625 crore (₹1,125 - ₹500).

context: Regulation 9(2): Any material alteration to the fund strategy shall be made with the consent of atleast two-thirds of unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund.

context: Regulation 14(g) (original): the client shall agree to obtain a rating from at least two different rating agencies for any issue of debt securities whose size is equal to or exceeds, rupees one hundred crores. question: Under the original SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, what was the mandatory dual-rating requirement for large debt issues, and when was it removed?
reference_answer: Under the original Regulation 14(g), a client was required to obtain ratings from at least two different credit rating agencies for any debt securities issue of Rs 100 crore or more. This mandatory dual-rating requirement was removed by the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2011, with effect from 27 December 2011. The 2011 amendment replaced this specific dual-rating obligation with a general requirement to obtain a rating 'in accordance with the relevant regulations.'

context: Regulation 15(1)(c): Category I and II of Alternative Investment Funds shall invest not more than twenty five per cent of the investable funds in an Investee Company directly or through investment in the units of other Alternative Investment Funds: Provided that large value funds for accredited investors of Category I and II may invest up to fifty percent of the investable funds in an investee company directly or through investment in the units of other Alternative Investment Funds.
question: What is the single-investee concentration limit for Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? Does this limit differ for large value funds for accredited investors?
reference_answer: Under Regulation 15(1)(c), Category I and II AIFs may invest not more than 25% of their investable funds in any single investee company (directly or through other AIF units). Large value funds for accredited investors in Category I and II may invest up to 50% of investable funds in a single investee company.

context: Regulation 30 (continual disclosures) was omitted by the SEBI (SAST) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2021, w.e.f. 1-4-2022. Prior to omission, Regulation 30 required every person holding 25%+ and all promoters to disclose their aggregate shareholding as of March 31 each year within 7 working days from year-end. Regulation 29(1) was also substituted by the same amendment, shifting from requiring disclosure only by the acquirer doing the acquisition to requiring disclosure by any acquirer (together with PAC) whose aggregate acquisition reaches 5% or more.
question: What happened to the annual continual disclosure requirement for promoters and major shareholders under SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, and when was it removed?
reference_answer: Regulation 30, which required every person holding 25% or more of voting rights and all promoters to disclose their aggregate shareholding as of March 31 each financial year (within 7 working days from year-end), was omitted by the Second Amendment Regulations, 2021, with effect from April 1, 2022. This was part of a broader overhaul of disclosure obligations, including changes to Regulation 29. The annual continual disclosure was likely subsumed into or replaced by disclosure requirements under the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015.

context: Annex I: Illustration 3: Computation of maximum eligible dividend for FY 20X1-X2. Net profit (PAT) for FY 20X1-X2 (A): Rs1,500 crore. Net NPAs as on March 31, 20X2 (B): Rs300 crore. Adjusted PAT, i.e., (C) = (A) - 50% of (B): Rs1,350 crore. Tier 1 capital ratio as on March 31, 20X1 (D): 24.36% (falls in Bucket B10). 75% of PAT (E): Rs1,125 crore. Maximum payable as per Table (100% of 1,350) (F): Rs1,350 crore. Maximum Eligible Dividend (G = Lower of E or F): Rs1,125 crore. Interim dividend paid for FY 20X1-20X2 (H): Rs500 crore. As the bank has already paid interim dividend of Rs500 crore, the final dividend shall not be more than (G) - (H).
question: In Illustration 3, a bank has PAT of Rs1,500 crore, Net NPA of Rs300 crore, Tier 1 ratio of 24.36%, and has already paid interim dividend of Rs500 crore. What is the maximum final dividend it may pay?
reference_answer: Rs625 crore (maximum eligible dividend of Rs1,125 crore minus interim dividend already paid of Rs500 crore)

context: Regulation 28E(m)(iv): [Category I ESG rating provider] maintain a minimum liquid net worth of rupees five crores at all times: at the time of making the application, the applicant shall have a minimum liquid net worth of the higher of, A. rupees ten crores, or B. addition of rupees five crores and the target on cumulative cash losses until breakeven.
question: A Category I ESG rating provider applicant projects cumulative cash losses of Rs 6 crore until breakeven. What is the minimum liquid net worth the applicant must demonstrate at the time of filing the registration application?
reference_answer: The minimum liquid net worth at application time is the higher of: (A) Rs 10 crore, or (B) Rs 5 crore + projected cumulative cash losses until breakeven = Rs 5 crore + Rs 6 crore = Rs 11 crore. Since Rs 11 crore > Rs 10 crore, the minimum required liquid net worth at application time is Rs 11 crore.

context: Regulation 16(1)(c): Category I Alternative Investment Funds shall not borrow funds directly or indirectly or engage in any leverage for the purpose of making investments or otherwise, except for borrowing funds to meet temporary funding requirements and day-to-day operational requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year and not more than ten percent of the investable funds.
question: Under what conditions may a Category I Alternative Investment Fund borrow funds under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? What are the specific restrictions on such borrowing?
reference_answer: Under Regulation 16(1)(c), Category I AIFs shall not borrow funds or engage in leverage for investment purposes. The only permitted borrowing is for temporary funding requirements and day-to-day operational requirements, subject to three cumulative conditions: (1) borrowing shall not be for more than thirty days at a time; (2) borrowing shall not occur on more than four occasions in a year; and (3) borrowing shall not exceed ten percent of the investable funds.

context: Regulation 7(1)(a) (pre-2020 Amendment): A professional qualification or graduate degree or post-graduate degree or post graduate diploma (minimum two years in duration) in finance, accountancy, business management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance or actuarial science or other financial services as may be specified from a university or an institution recognized by the Central Government or any State Government or a recognised foreign university or institution or association or a professional qualification by completing a Post Graduate Program in the Securities Market (Investment Advisory) from NISM of a duration not less than one year or a professional qualification by obtaining a CFA Charter from the CFA Institute. [As substituted w.e.f. 30-09-2020 and further updated w.e.f. 25-11-2025]: A graduate degree or any equivalent educational qualification from a recognized institution or CFA Charter, and relevant certification from NISM or accredited body.
question: How did the minimum qualification requirement for individual investment advisers under SEBI IA Regulations change with the 2020 amendment, and what further modification was made in 2025?
reference_answer: Under the original 2013 regulations, Regulation 7(1)(a) required a professional qualification or PG degree/diploma of minimum two years duration specifically in finance, accountancy, business management, commerce, economics, capital markets, banking, insurance, or actuarial science — or a CFA Charter. The SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020 (w.e.f. 30-09-2020) broadened this by permitting any professional qualification or graduate/post-graduate degree or diploma with no restriction on field of study, alongside NISM certification. The SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (w.e.f. 25-11-2025) further updated Regulation 7(1)(a) to require only a graduate degree (any discipline) or CFA Charter plus relevant NISM certification — removing the old requirement for a finance-specific discipline or work experience.

context: Regulation 8(10): Where the acquirer or persons acting in concert acquires shares of the target company during the period of twenty-six weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price under these regulations, the acquirer and persons acting in concert shall pay the difference between the highest acquisition price and the offer price, to all the shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer, within sixty days from the date of such acquisition.
question: Under Regulation 8(10), if an acquirer buys shares of the target company within 26 weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price, what obligation arises and within what timeframe must it be fulfilled?
reference_answer: The acquirer must pay the difference between the highest acquisition price and the open offer price to all shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer, within 60 days from the date of such acquisition. The obligation does not apply to acquisitions under another open offer, the Delisting Regulations, or ordinary open market purchases not involving negotiated transactions.

context: Regulation 13(h) (inserted by SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2024, w.e.f. 16-12-2024): the number of clients of a part-time investment adviser shall not exceed seventy-five in total at any point of time. Regulation 2(1)(qa) (inserted w.e.f. 16-12-2024): 'part-time investment adviser' means an individual or a firm, who for consideration, is engaged in the business of providing investment advice and is also engaged in any other business activity or employment.
question: When was the category of 'part-time investment adviser' and the 75-client limit introduced under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013, and what is the definition of a part-time investment adviser?
reference_answer: The concept of 'part-time investment adviser' and the 75-client limit were both introduced by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2024, with effect from 16 December 2024. A 'part-time investment adviser' is defined under Regulation 2(1)(qa) as an individual or a firm who, for consideration, is engaged in the business of providing investment advice and is also engaged in any other business activity or employment. Prior to this amendment, there was no regulatory distinction between full-time and part-time investment advisers.
